## Motivating question 

Do Americans consume more protein today than 20 years ago? 

We will use the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) to help us answer this question.

---


## Definitions 

+ Mean: average, center of data

$$\mathrm{mean}(x, y) = \frac{x + y}{2}$$
+ Standard deviation (sd): measure of spread of data around the mean

$$\mathrm{sd}(x, y) = \sqrt{\frac{(x- mean(x,y))^2 + (y-mean(x,y))^2}{2-1}} $$
+ Distribution: describes data (shape, center, spread) 

---

## The Normal Distribution (bell curve) 


```{r normal dist}
#| cache: true 


p_normal = 
  ggplot(data = tibble(x = c(-3, 3)), aes(x)) +
  geom_area(stat = "function", fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), 
            xlim = c(-3, 3), fill = "#56B4E9", alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), linewidth = 1.1) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())+
  labs(y = NULL, x = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-3, 3, 1))

p_normal 
```

```{r height dist}

bmx_joined %>%

  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")
```

## What's special about the Normal distribution? 


```{r normal1}
#| cache: true 

shade_df1 = tibble(
  x = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 500),
  y = dnorm(seq(-1, 1, length.out = 500), mean = 0, sd = 1)
)

shade_df2 = tibble(
  x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 500),
  y = dnorm(seq(-2, 2, length.out = 500), mean = 0, sd = 1)
)

shade_df3 = tibble(
  x = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 500),
  y = dnorm(seq(-3, 3, length.out = 500), mean = 0, sd = 1)
)

pn_1 = ggplot(data = tibble(x = c(-3, 3)), aes(x)) +
  geom_area(data = shade_df1, aes(x = x, y = y),
            fill = "#E69F00", alpha = 0.5) +
  annotate(geom = "label",
           x = 0, y = 0.3, color = "#E69F00",
           label = "68% of data") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank()) +
  labs(y = NULL, x = NULL) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 201, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1),
                linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-3, 3, 1))


pn_1 
```

# If we know data are Normally distributed, we can make statements about the values in the distribution

E.g.: "how unusual is this value?" 


---

### How unusual is my height? 


```{r unusual 1}
#| cache: true 
values = bmx_joined %>% 
  filter(age_in_years_at_screening >= 18, gender == "Female") %>% 
  mutate(height_in = standing_height_cm / 2.54) %>% 
  select(height_in) %>% 
  drop_na() %>% 
  pull()
dens = density(values)
y_val = dens$y[which.min(abs(dens$x - (5*12)))]
mean_ht = mean(values)
sd_ht = sd(values, na.rm = TRUE)


p = 
  bmx_joined %>% 
  filter(age_in_years_at_screening >= 18, gender == "Female") %>% 
  mutate(height_in = standing_height_cm / 2.54) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = height_in)) + 
  geom_density(linewidth = 1.3, color = "#CC79A7") + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(54, 78, 3),
                     labels = seq(4.5, 6.5, 0.25),
                     limits = c(52, 76)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0)) +
  labs(x = "Height (ft)", y = "Number of people", title = "Height among American female adults",
       subtitle = "From the 2021 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey")  +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none",
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank()) 



p

```

---

### How unusual is my height? 

```{r unusual2}
#| cache: true 
p2 = p + 
  geom_labelvline(aes(xintercept = mean_ht), linetype = "dashed",
                  label = "Mean", angle = 90, color = "darkgrey") + 
  geom_textvline(aes(xintercept = mean_ht - sd_ht), linetype = "dotted",
                      label = "-1 SD", color = "darkgrey") + 
  geom_textvline(aes(xintercept = mean_ht + sd_ht), linetype = "dotted",
                      label = "+1 SD", color = "darkgrey") + 
  geom_textvline(aes(xintercept = mean_ht - 2*sd_ht), linetype = "dotted",
                      label = "-2 SD", color = "darkgrey") + 
  geom_textvline(aes(xintercept = mean_ht + 2*sd_ht), linetype = "dotted",
                      label = "+2 SD", color = "darkgrey") + 
  geom_textvline(aes(xintercept = mean_ht - 3*sd_ht), linetype = "dotted",
                      label = "-3 SD", color = "darkgrey") + 
  geom_textvline(aes(xintercept = mean_ht + 3*sd_ht), linetype = "dotted",
                      label = "+3 SD", color = "darkgrey") + 
  annotate(geom = "label", x = 6*12, y = 0.12, label = expression(Height~ "~" ~ N(5.27, 0.23^2)), parse = TRUE)

p2
```

# What about the mean of samples from non-Normal data? 

---

### Protein data: means 

```{r protein pop1}
#| cache: true 

xy_df = expand_grid(x = 1:71, y = 1:71) %>% 
  slice(1:nrow(protein_df23))

dots = 
  protein_df23 %>% 
  bind_cols(xy_df) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x, y, color = protein_gm)) + 
  geom_point(size = 0.5) + 
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void() +
  scale_color_viridis(option = "B", name = "Protein (g)",
                      limits = c(0, 350)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") + 
  labs(title = "Population of protein values (N=4986)") + 
  annotate(geom = "label", size = 4,
           x = 71 / 2, y = 71 / 2,
           label = glue::glue("Mean = ", round(mean(protein_df23$protein_gm), 0), " g"),
           fill = "white")

plot_grid(dots, NULL, align = "v", rel_widths = c(1,1), ncol = 2)



## represent our data  points

# show the mean x 3 
# then show the sampling distribution
```

```{ojs}
data = FileAttachment("protein_df.csv").csv({ typed: true })

viewof sample_size = Inputs.range(
  [2, 100], 
  {value: 50, step: 1, label: "Sample size:"}
)

//viewof n_samples = Inputs.range(
//  [10, 1000], 
  //{value: 500, step: 10, label: "Number samples:"}
//)

sample_means = {
  // Dependency tracking: re-run when these change
  sample_size;
  
  // Safety check: ensure data is loaded
  if (!data || data.length === 0) return [];
  
  // Safety check: ensure column exists (Case Sensitive!)
  if (typeof data[0].protein_gm === "undefined") {
    return ["Error: Column 'protein' not found in data"];
  }

  const means = [];
  // Create a local copy of the array to shuffle
  // We do this inside the loop or use a specific shuffler to ensure 
  // we are sampling from the full population every time.
  const popArray = Array.from(data); 

  for (let i = 0; i < 500; i++) {
    // 1. Shuffle a clean copy of the population
    // 2. Slice the first n elements (Sampling WITHOUT replacement)
    const sample = d3.shuffle([...popArray]).slice(0, sample_size);

    // 3. Compute mean
    const m = d3.mean(sample, d => d.protein_gm);
    means.push(m);
  }

  return means;
}

normalCurve = {
  if (sample_means.length < 2 || !data) return [];
  
  // 1. Get Population Statistics
  const popMean = d3.mean(data, d => d.protein_gm);
  const popSD = d3.deviation(data, d => d.protein_gm);
  
  // 2. Calculate Standard Error (The predicted width of the sampling distribution)
  // Formula: Population SD / sqrt(n)
  const se = popSD / Math.sqrt(sample_size2);

  // 3. Determine range for the curve (centered on popMean)
  const minX = popMean - (4 * se);
  const maxX = popMean + (4 * se);
  
  // Create a smooth grid of X values
  const grid = d3.range(minX, maxX, (maxX - minX) / 200);
  
  // Normal Density Function using Population Mean and Standard Error
  const pdf = (x) => (1 / (se * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))) * Math.exp(-0.5 * Math.pow((x - popMean) / se, 2));
  
  return grid.map(x => ({x: x, y: pdf(x)}));
}

// 6. PLOT
{
  const bins = d3.bin().thresholds(20)(sample_means);
  const n = sample_means.length;

  return Plot.plot({
    width: 900,
    height: 500,
    caption: `Distribution of sample means (n=${sample_size2})`,
    
    // Global font style
    style: {
      fontSize: "18px",
      overflow: "visible" 
    },
    marginLeft: 60,
    marginBottom: 60,
    marginTop: 30,

    // DEFINE LEGEND COLORS
    color: {
      domain: ["Sample Mean", "Population Mean", "Normal Curve"],
      range: ["#D55E00", "black", "#CC79A7"],
      legend: true
    },
    marks: [
      // Histogram (Manual Density Calculation)
      Plot.rectY(bins, {
        x1: "x0", 
        x2: "x1", 
        // Density Formula: Count / (Total Samples * Bin Width)
        y: d => d.length / (n * (d.x1 - d.x0)), 
        fill: "#56B4E9", 
        fillOpacity: 0.5,
        tip: true,
        title: d => `Count: ${d.length}\nDensity: ${(d.length / (n * (d.x1 - d.x0))).toFixed(3)}`
      }),
      
      // The Normal Curve Overlay
      Plot.line(normalCurve, {
        x: "x",
        y: "y",
        stroke: () => "Normal Curve",
        strokeWidth: 3
      }),

      // The Mean of the Sampling Distribution (Red Line)
      Plot.ruleX([d3.mean(sample_means)], { 
        stroke: () => "Sample Mean", 
        strokeWidth: 3,
        title: d => `Sample Mean: ${d.toFixed(2)}` 
      }),
      
      // The True Population Mean (Black dashed line)
      data && data.length > 0 ? Plot.ruleX([d3.mean(data, d => d.protein_gm)], { 
        stroke: () => "Population Mean", 
        strokeDasharray: "4,4",
        strokeWidth: 2,
        opacity: 0.8,
        title: d => `True Pop Mean: ${d.toFixed(2)}`
      }) : null
    ],
    
    // AXIS CONFIGUprotein_gmN
    x: { 
      label: "Protein (sample mean)", 
      tickFormat: ".1f",
      labelOffset: 50
    },
    y: { 
      label: "Density", 
    }
  })
}

```

```{ojs}
data2 = FileAttachment("income_df.csv").csv({ typed: true })

viewof sample_size2 = Inputs.range(
  [2, 100], 
  {value: 50, step: 1, label: "Sample size:"}
)

//)

sample_means2 = {
  // Dependency tracking: re-run when these change
  sample_size2;
  
  // Safety check: ensure data is loaded
  if (!data2 || data2.length === 0) return [];
  
  // Safety check: ensure column exists (Case Sensitive!)
  if (typeof data2[0].ratio === "undefined") {
    return ["Error: Column 'ratio' not found in data"];
  }

  const means = [];
  // Create a local copy of the array to shuffle
  // We do this inside the loop or use a specific shuffler to ensure 
  // we are sampling from the full population every time.
  const popArray = Array.from(data2); 

  for (let i = 0; i < 500; i++) {
    // 1. Shuffle a clean copy of the population
    // 2. Slice the first n elements (Sampling WITHOUT replacement)
    const sample = d3.shuffle([...popArray]).slice(0, sample_size2);

    // 3. Compute mean
    const m = d3.mean(sample, d => d.ratio);
    means.push(m);
  }

  return means;
}


// 5. CALCULATE NORMAL CURVE (THEORETICAL)
// We now generate the curve based on the Population Parameters, not the sample.
// This shows the Theoretical prediction of the CLT.
normalCurve2 = {
  if (sample_means2.length < 2 || !data2) return [];
  
  // 1. Get Population Statistics
  const popMean = d3.mean(data2, d => d.ratio);
  const popSD = d3.deviation(data2, d => d.ratio);
  
  // 2. Calculate Standard Error (The predicted width of the sampling distribution)
  // Formula: Population SD / sqrt(n)
  const se = popSD / Math.sqrt(sample_size2);

  // 3. Determine range for the curve (centered on popMean)
  const minX = popMean - (4 * se);
  const maxX = popMean + (4 * se);
  
  // Create a smooth grid of X values
  const grid = d3.range(minX, maxX, (maxX - minX) / 200);
  
  // Normal Density Function using Population Mean and Standard Error
  const pdf = (x) => (1 / (se * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))) * Math.exp(-0.5 * Math.pow((x - popMean) / se, 2));
  
  return grid.map(x => ({x: x, y: pdf(x)}));
}

// 6. PLOT
{
  const bins = d3.bin().thresholds(20)(sample_means2);
  const n = sample_means2.length;

  return Plot.plot({
    width: 900,
    height: 500,
    caption: `Distribution of sample means (n=${sample_size2})`,
    
    // Global font style
    style: {
      fontSize: "18px",
      overflow: "visible" 
    },
    marginLeft: 60,
    marginBottom: 60,
    marginTop: 30,

    // DEFINE LEGEND COLORS
    color: {
      domain: ["Sample Mean", "Population Mean", "Normal Curve"],
      range: ["#D55E00", "black", "#CC79A7"],
      legend: true
    },
    marks: [
      // Histogram (Manual Density Calculation)
      Plot.rectY(bins, {
        x1: "x0", 
        x2: "x1", 
        // Density Formula: Count / (Total Samples * Bin Width)
        y: d => d.length / (n * (d.x1 - d.x0)), 
        fill: "#56B4E9", 
        fillOpacity: 0.5,
        tip: true,
        title: d => `Count: ${d.length}\nDensity: ${(d.length / (n * (d.x1 - d.x0))).toFixed(3)}`
      }),
      
      // The Normal Curve Overlay
      Plot.line(normalCurve2, {
        x: "x",
        y: "y",
        stroke: () => "Normal Curve",
        strokeWidth: 3
      }),

      // The Mean of the Sampling Distribution (Red Line)
      Plot.ruleX([d3.mean(sample_means2)], { 
        stroke: () => "Sample Mean", 
        strokeWidth: 3,
        title: d => `Sample Mean: ${d.toFixed(2)}` 
      }),
      
      // The True Population Mean (Black dashed line)
      data2 && data2.length > 0 ? Plot.ruleX([d3.mean(data2, d => d.ratio)], { 
        stroke: () => "Population Mean", 
        strokeDasharray: "4,4",
        strokeWidth: 2,
        opacity: 0.8,
        title: d => `True Pop Mean: ${d.toFixed(2)}`
      }) : null
    ],
    
    // AXIS CONFIGURATION
    x: { 
      label: "Ratio of income to poverty (sample mean)", 
      tickFormat: ".1f",
      labelOffset: 50
    },
    y: { 
      label: "Density", 
    }
  })
}
```

## Central Limit Theorem Definition 

The distribution of the sample means is approximately Normal, regardless of the shape of the population distribution, provided the sample size is sufficiently large $(n \geq 30)$ 

---


## Central Limit Theorem

The distribution of the sample means is approximately Normal, regardless of the shape of the population distribution, as long as the sample size is big enough $(n \geq 30)$  !!!

$$\mathrm{sample} \hspace{.05in} \mathrm{means} \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\mathrm{mean = pop mean}, \mathrm{sd = pop sd}/\sqrt{\mathrm{sample \hspace{.05in} size}}\big) $$ 
---



## So what? 

</br>

+ Usually, all we have is the sample mean ($\overline{X}$)
+ We would like to use that to learn about the population mean (μ)
+ Now we know the distribution for $\overline{X}$, so we can do that 
+ **Without** knowing the shape of the population data 

---

### Example 

Protein, again

Let's treat the individuals as the population, but pretend we only observe a sample of size $n=50$ 

```{r clt example}
#| echo: true 
#| cache: true 

set.seed(4367)
sample_50 = sample(protein_values, size = 50, replace = FALSE)

sample_mean = mean(sample_50); sample_mean
```

We got a sample mean of `r round(sample_mean, 1)`. If the true mean in the population were 60 grams, how surprising would it be to get a sample mean this far from 60?

(This is *hypothesis testing*)

---

### Example 



If the true mean in the population is 60, and we repeatedly took samples of 50 people, then the CLT tells us that the sample means would be Normally distributed: 

$$\bar{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(60, \sigma / \sqrt{50})$$ 




---

### Example 

If the true mean in the population is 60, and we repeatedly took samples of 50 people, then the CLT tells us that the sample means would be Normally distributed: 

$$\bar{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(60, \sigma / \sqrt{50})$$ 

What about $\sigma$? 

For now, let's pretend we know it. 

```{r sd}
#| echo: true 

sigma = sd(protein_values); sigma

```

---

### Example 

If the true mean in the population is 60, and we repeatedly took samples of 50 people, then the CLT tells us that the sample means would be Normally distributed: 

$$\bar{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(60, \sigma / \sqrt{50})$$ 

What about $\sigma$? 

For now, let's pretend we know it. 

```{r sd2}
#| echo: true 

sigma = sd(protein_values); sigma

```

$$\overline{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(60, 33.8 / \sqrt{50} = 4.78)$$ 


---


### Example

Let's plot that hypothetical distribution as the pink curve: 

```{r ex1}
#| cache: true 
sim_values = rnorm(100000, mean = 60, sd = sigma / sqrt(50)) %>% 
  as_tibble()
pop_mean = 60
dens2 = density(sim_values$value)
y_val = dens2$y[which.min(abs(dens2$x - (sample_mean)))]
se = sigma / sqrt(50)
y_val1 = dens2$y[which.min(abs(dens2$x-(pop_mean + se)))]
y_val2 = dens2$y[which.min(abs(dens2$x-(pop_mean - se)))]
y_val3 = dens2$y[which.min(abs(dens2$x-sample_mean))]
opp = pop_mean - (sample_mean - pop_mean)
y_val4 = dens2$y[which.min(abs(dens2$x-opp))]

pr =
  sim_values %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) + 
  geom_density(linewidth = 1.3, color = "#CC79A7") +
  labs(x = "Protein (g)", y = NULL, title = "Distribution of sample means") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(50, 100, 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0)) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none",
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank()) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = pop_mean), linetype = "dashed", color = "darkgrey") +
  annotate(geom = "label", x = pop_mean, y = 0.05, 
           label = glue::glue("Mean = ", round(pop_mean, 1))) + 
  annotate(geom = "segment", 
           x = pop_mean + se, xend = pop_mean + se, y = 0, 
               yend = y_val1, linetype = "dashed", color = "darkgrey") + 
  annotate(geom = "label", x = pop_mean + se, y = 0.025, 
           label = glue::glue("+1 SD (", round(se, 1), ")")) +
  annotate(geom = "segment", x = pop_mean - se, 
           xend = pop_mean - se, y = 0, 
               yend = y_val2, linetype = "dashed", color = "darkgrey") + 
  annotate(geom = "label", x = pop_mean - se, y = 0.025, 
           label = glue::glue("-1 SD (", round(se, 1), ")")) 



pr

```

---

### Example 

And then add the value we observe (our sample mean) as a blue dot: 

```{r add mean}
#| cache: true 
pr + 
   annotate(geom = "point", 
           x = sample_mean, y = y_val3, color = "#0072B2", 
           size = 4)
```


---

### Example 

::: {.incremental}
+ 
If the population mean were really 60, is it plausible that we would see a sample mean this far from 60 just by chance?

+ We don’t care only about values that are higher than 60 or only lower than 60: either direction would make us doubt the hypothesis that the true mean is 60.

+ So we ask a two-sided question:
  *How likely is it to be at least this far from 60 in either direction?*

:::

---

### Example

```{r 2 sided}
#| cache: true 

dens_df2 = 
  tibble(x = dens2$x,
         y = dens2$y)
pr + 
  geom_area(data = dens_df2 %>% filter(x <= opp),
            aes(x, y = y), alpha = 0.3,
            fill = "#0072B2") +
  geom_area(data = dens_df2 %>% filter(x > sample_mean),
            aes(x, y = y), alpha = 0.3, 
            fill = "#0072B2")  +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1.3, color = "#CC79A7") +
  annotate(geom = "point", 
           x = sample_mean, y = y_val3, color = "#0072B2", 
           size = 4) +
  annotate(geom = "point", x = opp,
            y = y_val4, color = "#0072B2", 
           size = 4) 
  
```

---

### Example 

<span style="color:#0072B2;">Blue shaded area represents:</span>

If the population mean is 60, how likely is it we would observe the sample mean we got? 

```{r pnorm ex1}
#| echo: true
#| cache: true

2 * pnorm(60 - (sample_mean - 60), mean = 60, sd = sigma / sqrt(50)) * 100

```

---

### Example 

<span style="color:#0072B2;">Blue shaded area represents:</span>

If the population mean is 60, how likely is it we would observe the sample mean we got? 

```{r pnorm ex}
#| echo: true
#| cache: true

2 * pnorm(60 - (sample_mean - 60), mean = 60, sd = sigma / sqrt(50)) * 100

```

We conclude it's plausible that our population mean is 60
